newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean inventories worrisome, despite Q1 growth.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean inventories worrisome, despite Q1 growth.

text.p: First quarter economic growth figures announced by the Bank of Korea on Thursday were better than expected but economists warned that manufacturers' high inventories could delay South Korea's economic turnaround.
They said the financial troubles surfacing around several high-profile conglomerates or "chaebol" would also slow economic activity and growth.
Gross domestic product (GDP) grew a real 5.4 percent during the first quarter against 7.8 percent a year before, the central bank said.
"Growth was higher than expected as an inventory adjustment has not yet been finished," Paeng Dong-joon, BOK's statistics director, told reporters.
The central bank earlier had forecast GDP growth would come in at just over 5.0 percent, while research bodies said it would register between 4.8 and 5.0 percent.

Most worrisome were manufacturing inventories, which rose 13.8 percent in the first quarter. That increase was down from the 19.1 percent rise a year earlier but more than double the 5.0 percent rise for first quarter 1995, he said.
A better rate would be 8.0 to 9.0 percent, Paeng said.

"Korean companies need to reduce their inventories when the economy is on a downward curve. If not, the slowdown in the nation's economy will be prolonged," said Lee Yong-man, senior economist at LG Economic Research Institute.
A central bank statement attributed rising inventories in the first quarter to sluggish domestic consumption and a decline in facilities and construction investment.
Analysts said the spectre of corporate defaults this year was blocking a turnaround.

The nation's 25th largest chaebol, the New Core Group, said on Thursday it was seeking 90 billion won ($101 million) in fresh loans from several banks. Its finance manager denied reports of troubles and insisted the group was not in danger of defaulting on its debt payments.
New Core, a distribution and retailing giant, has 18 affiliates, none of which is listed.
South Korea has been rocked by the collapse of Hanbo Steel in January and Sammi Steel Co in March, both under heavy debts incurred mainly by excessive expansion.
Since then four chaebol, including sixth-ranked Ssangyong Group, have said they were experiencing serious liquidity problems and pledged to restructure.
"There is no doubt the corporate troubles will hurt the economy," said Rhee Namuh, head of research at Dongbang Peregrine.
Analysts said restructuring was a good idea.
"They are in trouble because the bubbles in the once fast-growing economy have begun easing," said Rhee Kang-ok, senior economist at Dongsuh Economic Research Institute.
Analysts were divided on the economy's immediate outlook.
Dongsuh and LG have forecast the economy would bottom out this summer on rising exports, rebounding export prices of major export items, the yen's strength and falling oil prices.
LG forecast 5.7 percent GDP growth for the whole of this year and Dongsuh put it at six percent.
But Rhee of Dongbang Peregrine disagreed.
"A recovery will be delayed until 1998," he said. "The Korean economy will have to work off the excesses such as overcapacity in virtually all sectors of industry. This will be a painful process."
He forecast 4.1 percent GDP growth this year.
(Conversion $1 = 890 won)
